prompt:
Our feature-flag code only supports one shared global registry, which makes it impossible to use an independent set of flags (per-tenant, per-test, whatever) without it leaking into the same global state everyone else uses. Replace the hidden singleton with real dependency injection, while keeping every bit of the current module-level convenience API working exactly as it does today.

Concretely:
- Expose the shared global `FeatureFlags` instance that `flags.py` already keeps internally as a public module attribute, `flags.default_registry`, so other modules can reference the exact same object instead of only reaching it through the module-level functions.
- `flags.enable(name)` / `flags.disable(name)` / `flags.is_enabled(name)` / `flags.all_flags()` must keep behaving exactly as they do now - under the hood they operate on `flags.default_registry`, and callers of these four functions should see no difference at all.
- Give `gating.run_if_enabled` and `reporting.build_report` an optional `registry=` parameter. When it's omitted, they must operate on `flags.default_registry` - the same shared instance the module-level functions use, not a new, separate `FeatureFlags()`. When a caller passes their own `FeatureFlags` instance, they operate on that instance instead, completely independently of the global one.
- Likewise, give `cli.py`'s `main` an optional `registry=` parameter (`main(argv, registry=None)`) with the same fallback-to-global behavior, so it can be driven against an isolated registry without touching global state.
- `FeatureFlags.all_flags()` must keep returning a plain `dict` copy (not a live view) - mutating the returned dict must never affect the registry.
- Preserve this existing distinction precisely while you refactor the storage: `all_flags()` includes every name that has ever been passed to `enable`/`disable` (mapped to its current True/False state, so a flag that was explicitly disabled but never enabled still shows up, as `False`), while a name nobody has ever touched is absent from `all_flags()`/the report entirely, even though `is_enabled` still reports `False` for it, same as today.
- `enable`/`disable`/`is_enabled` (both the module-level functions and the `FeatureFlags` methods) must keep raising `TypeError("flag name must be a string")` for a non-string `name`.
